name: validation layer (P19)

R4.why: Own time, own kit, the stack's own governance.

R9.why: Only the method is published; rules and runs stay private.

answers: The stack keeps adding layers on a first answer. The validation layer asks the architect's questions before a new layer or major version is built, and records the answer with its spec.

answers.start: Ask the architect's questions before a new layer is built.
whys: Because new layers and versions get added on a first answer: the Saboteur reached a six-layer chain before a consolidation.
Because nothing in the stack asks what a layer is worth, or what it replaces, before code is written.
Because those questions lived in a checklist page outside the stack, used by one person on demand.
Because the checklist was built for a job interview failure (approaching a role as an engineer, not an architect) and never connected to the stack's own governance.
Because the stack had no layer whose job is to judge proposals; HAL judges actions and the agents check files, not decisions.

answers:
No AI inside the engine.
No blocking gate in the first slice (advise first).
No private rules, guard words or past runs in the public repo.
No second copy of the method: the page's data block stays the one source.
James sees a score, the flags and the three biggest gains for each proposed layer before code exists, and the run is kept with the layer's spec for anyone who reads it later.
3 new layers or major versions each have a recorded run with a verdict before their code, by 2027-02-28; and at least 1 run changes or kills a decision.
James decides. The agents and the VPS check would read the runs later. Nobody outside James is waiting for it yet.
James owns it and signs off its freezes.
James runs it before a new layer; the engine runs offline in seconds. Nothing runs on a timer, so there is no 3am call.
If it is wrong, a weak layer gets a good score and is built anyway; the harm is wasted build time, not lost data.
James's time per run (about 30 minutes for a Full run). The engine and tests cost nothing to run: local Python and Node.
Saves the rework of layers that should not have been built; doing nothing costs another chain like the Saboteur's before its consolidation, and the 1.0.0 consolidation took most of a day.
An architecture decision record template, a design review by a person, an AI review, or doing nothing and relying on memory. Could reuse an open-source ADR template instead of the checklist.
Spare time only. The method must stay one source (the page). Nothing private in a public repo. The stack's rules: version, never overwrite, James signs.
Run files with answers about the stack's own designs. James's rules and past runs are personal and stay in his home folder.
Python for the engine; Node only for the parity tests; the page on James's laptop as the source of truth. All local and replaceable.
One run per new layer, a few a month. At 10x it is still files on disk; the Patterns view gets more useful, not slower.

1. Port the page's scoring to Python, the page staying the source
2. Use an open-source ADR template and no scoring
3. Call the page's own script under Node from the stack
4. Don't build it, park it: keep the checklist outside the stack

The port means two implementations, kept in step by parity tests. The ADR template has no scoring or flags. Node at run time would make Node a dependency of every layer that asks. Parking keeps the stack without a judge of proposals.

answers.chosen: Port the page's scoring to Python, the page staying the source
answers.rejected: ADR template; Node at run time; park it
answers.reason: Python is what every layer already runs; the parity tests keep the port honest against the page.
answers.downside: Two implementations of the scoring, and the parity tests only run where the private page is.
answers.trigger: If parity fails on more than 2 runs in a month, call the page under Node instead.

answers: The engine, the parity tests, and one run on the proposal itself, done by 2026-12-21.

The page's logic can be run outside a browser.
The Python engine gives the same scores as the page.
The method can be published without any work material.
Run the page's logic outside a browser under Node and compare scores with the Python engine on every synthetic run; a test refuses any published method that holds a guarded word or work material.
The parity test fails when the engine and the page disagree on a score; the privacy test fails when a published file holds work material.
The engine and the page disagree on a score, so a run is judged differently in the stack than on the page.

answers.start: The engine and the page disagree on a score.
whys: Because a rule changed on the page and the Python port was not changed.
Because the parity tests only run where the private page is.

answers: The worst misuse is publishing James's private rules or runs by accident; the extractor refuses a method with a guarded word, and the profile is git-ignored.
When the page changes a rule, run the extractor and the parity tests; fix the port until they pass, and record it as a new version.
James approves every freeze. The page's data block is the one source; the method file is generated from it; the CHANGELOG records each change.
The page, the method file and the spec let someone else run it. A handover capsule is not written yet.
The README shows one command that scores a run in seconds.

answers.signal: 3 recorded runs by 2027-02-28 with no decision changed or killed by any of them
answers.then: James decides: keep it as advice, or retire it to the archive.

evidence.fig: Engine runs in under 1 second per run
